title: Configuring SSL Encryption Between SAP ABAP Application Servers and SAP HANA
author: PB91
text:
Introduction 
 This blog documents the steps required to configure SSL/TLS encryption between SAP ABAP application servers and an SAP HANA database, using a certificate signed by an external Certificate Authority (CA). This is a common requirement in enterprise migrations and security hardening projects where the default SAP-generated certificates are replaced with organisation-specific ones. 
 The configuration covered here implements one-way TLS — the HANA database server authenticates itself to the ABAP application layer. sapcli.pse on each ABAP node serves as the trust store , allowing the ABAP kernel to verify HANA's certificate during the TLS handshake. This guide assumes you are working on a Linux-based SAP system with SAP CommonCryptoLib installed.

 1. Why 5HP Reversal Has No Standard Path 
 5HP uses the NBIC purchase order type. Three constraints shape the reversal problem: 

 No Return STO for NBIC. SAP has confirmed that the aICO framework does not support a Return STO document type. The standard Return PO path for external supplier returns does not apply to intercompany transfers — the financial and stock account logic is fundamentally different.

title: Reversing the 5HP NBIC Intercompany STO in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
author: Qi_Liu
text:
Scope Item: 5HP — Advanced Intercompany Stock Transfer 
 Document Type: NBIC (Cross-Company, Delivery-Linked) 
 Verified on: SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 
 Test Date: 2026-09-22 / 2026-10-19 
 1. Why 5HP Reversal Has No Standard Path 
 5HP uses the NBIC purchase order type. Three constraints shape the reversal problem: 

 No Return STO for NBIC. SAP has confirmed that the aICO framework does not support a Return STO document type. The standard Return PO path for external supplier returns does not apply to intercompany transfers — the financial and stock account logic is fundamentally different. 

 The delivery chain is mandatory in both directions. Because NBIC requires OBD → PGI → IBD → GR in the forward flow, the reversal must mirror this in strict reverse. Skipping or reordering steps produces VL/066 locks or status inconsistencies. 

 Two WL-linked goods movements require UI intervention. The GRRV (MT107, WL-linked blocked stock GR) and the GIIV (Post GI from Issuing SiT, WL-linked) cannot be cancelled via OData API. Both must be cancelled through the Monitor Value Chains Fiori app before the delivery documents can be deleted. 
 2. Verified Reversal Sequence 
 Document chain (Full 5HP variant): 
 STO [NBIC — Plant 1310 → Plant 1320]
 └─→ OBD
 │ PGI material documents:
 │ ├── MT681 (GIOD): Plant 1310 unrestricted -1, transit +1
 │ └── MT107 (GRRV, WL-linked): Plant 1320 GR blocked +1
 ├─→ IV2 [auto-generated after PGI]
 └─→ IBD [auto-generated after PGI]
 │ IBD GR material documents (single GR posting):
 │ ├── MT685 (GIIV, WL-linked): Plant 1310 SiT -1
 │ ├── MT107 (GRRV, WL-linked): Plant 1320 GR blocked +1
 │ └── MT109 (GRID): Plant 1320 GR blocked -1 → unrestricted +1 
 Full 5HP identification: In Monitor Value Chains, check whether a "Post GI from Issuing SiT (GIIV)" step appears after PGI. If yes, the IBD GR creates all three material documents (GIIV + GRRV + GRID) together. If not, this is the simple variant and only MT109 (GRID) needs to be reversed in Step 2. 
 Reversal execution order: 
 Step 1 — Cancel IV2 billing document [API ✅]
Step 2 — ReverseGoodsReceipt on IBD [API ✅ — reverses MT109 + MT685 atomically]
Step 3 — Cancel GRRV (MT107, WL-linked) [UI ✅ — Monitor Value Chains, after Step 2]
Step 4 — Cancel GIIV (Post GI from Issuing SiT) [UI ✅ — Monitor Value Chains, after Step 3]
Step 5 — Delete IBD [API ✅ — HTTP 204, Steps 3+4 required first]
Step 6 — ReverseGoodsIssue on OBD [API ✅ — after Step 5]
Step 7 — Delete OBD [API ✅ — HTTP 204, after Step 6]
Step 8 — SetItemToDeleted on STO item [API ✅] 
 3. Authentication and Session Architecture 
 All write operations use a Communication User via Basic Auth, provisioned through the relevant Communication Arrangement ( SAP_COM_0022 for Delivery Processing Integration, SAP_COM_0006 for Material Documents, SAP_COM_0A80 for Stock Transport Orders, SAP_COM_0A95 for Billing Documents, SAP_COM_0734 for Outbound Delivery GI). 
 $user = "SALES_AGENT_API"
$pass = '<your-password>'
$base = "https://<your-tenant>-api.s4hana.cloud.sap"
$cookieJar = "$env:TEMP\session_$(Get-Date -Format 'HHmmss').txt"

$ibdRoot = "$base/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_INBOUND_DELIVERY_SRV;v=2"
$obdRoot = "$base/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_OUTBOUND_DELIVERY_SRV;v=2"
$stoRoot = "$base/sap/opu/odata4/sap/api_stocktransportorder/srvd_a2x/sap/stocktransportorder/0001" 
 Session rule: Every POST must use curl -c/-b <cookie-jar> to maintain session continuity. The CSRF token fetch, entity GET, and FunctionImport POST must share the same HTTP session. 
 CSRF token fetch template: 
 # Fetch token against the target service root entity set (not base URL)
$fetchOut = & curl.exe -s -D - -o NUL `
 -u "${user}:${pass}" `
 -H "x-csrf-token: fetch" `
 -H "Accept: application/json" `
 -c $cookieJar `
 "$ibdRoot/A_InbDeliveryHeader"
$csrf = ($fetchOut | Select-String "(?i)x-csrf-token:\s*(.+)").Matches.Groups[1].Value.Trim() 
 Each service ( API_INBOUND_DELIVERY_SRV , API_OUTBOUND_DELIVERY_SRV , api_stocktransportorder ) requires its own CSRF token fetched in a separate session. Do not reuse a token across services. 
 4. Step 1 — Cancel Intercompany Invoice (IV2) 
 Fiori: Manage Billing Documents → select IV2 → Cancel 
 API: 
 GET /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BILLING_DOCUMENT_SRV/A_BillingDocument('<IV2_NUMBER>')
 ?$format=json
# Extract __metadata.etag from response

POST /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BILLING_DOCUMENT_SRV/Cancel?BillingDocument='<IV2_NUMBER>'
 &$format=json
x-csrf-token: <fetched>
If-Match: <etag_from_GET>
Accept: application/json 
 ⚠️ ETag required: The Cancel FunctionImport returns HTTP 428 if If-Match is missing. Always do a GET first to retrieve the ETag, then pass it in the POST. Pass BillingDocument as a query string parameter — embedding it in the URL path returns HTTP 404. 
 Check all IV2 documents for the OBD before cancelling: 
 GET /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BILLING_DOCUMENT_SRV/A_BillingDocumentItem
 ?$filter=ReferenceSDDocument eq '<OBD_NUMBER>'
 &$select=BillingDocument,BillingDocumentItem,ReferenceSDDocument
 &$format=json 
 Then verify each billing document's status: 
 GET /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BILLING_DOCUMENT_SRV/A_BillingDocument('<BillingDocument>')
 ?$select=BillingDocument,BillingDocumentType,OverallBillingStatus,CancelledBillingDocument
 &$format=json 
 BillingDocumentType = IV2 , OverallBillingStatus = C → active invoice, cancel this 
 BillingDocumentType = IV2S → cancellation document (expected, no action) 
 BillingDocumentType = IV2 with empty CancelledBillingDocument and OverallBillingStatus = A → re-created by background job, also cancel this 
 All IV2 documents must be in cancelled state before Step 6. 
 ⚠️ Billing re-creation trap: After cancelling IV2, the OBD's OverallIntcoBillingStatus resets to A , making it eligible for re-billing. If a background billing job ( BILLING_DOCUMENT_RUN ) runs before Step 6, it will create a new IV2 and block ReverseGoodsIssue again. Execute Steps 1 through 6 in a single uninterrupted session — no idle time between them. 
 5. Step 2 — Reverse Goods Receipt on IBD (GRID + GIIV) 
 Service: API_INBOUND_DELIVERY_SRV (OData V2) 
 Prerequisite: IBD OverallGoodsMovementStatus = C 
 In the Full 5HP variant, this single API call atomically reverses: 
 MT109 (GRID): removes stock from receiving plant unrestricted inventory 
 MT685 (GIIV): restores SiT +1 at issuing plant (required for Step 6 to succeed) 
 The WL-linked MT107 (GRRV) is intentionally not reversed here — it is handled in Step 3. 
 $ibd = "<IBD_NUMBER>"

# Fetch CSRF token for IBD service
$fetchOut = & curl.exe -s -D - -o NUL `
 -u "${user}:${pass}" `
 -H "x-csrf-token: fetch" `
 -H "Accept: application/json" `
 -c $cookieJar `
 "$ibdRoot/A_InbDeliveryHeader"
$csrf = ($fetchOut | Select-String "(?i)x-csrf-token:\s*(.+)").Matches.Groups[1].Value.Trim()

# ReverseGoodsReceipt — do NOT include If-Match (returns HTTP 501 if added)
& curl.exe -s -X POST `
 -u "${user}:${pass}" `
 -H "x-csrf-token: $csrf" `
 -H "Accept: application/json" `
 -b $cookieJar -c $cookieJar `
 -w "`nHTTP:%{http_code}" `
 "$ibdRoot/ReverseGoodsReceipt?DeliveryDocument='${ibd}'&ActualGoodsMovementDate=datetime'<REVERSAL_DATE>T00%3A00%3A00'&`$format=json"
# Expected: HTTP 200, IBD OverallGoodsMovementStatus → A 
 Verified response (HTTP 200): 
 { "d": { "results": [] } } 
 An empty results array confirms clean reversal with no warnings. 
 ⚠️ Critical — never cancel GRID directly: Cancelling MT109 via Monitor Value Chains or API_MATERIAL_DOCUMENT_SRV without going through ReverseGoodsReceipt leaves MT685 (GIIV) unreversed. This depletes SiT to 0 at the issuing plant, causing VL/624 on the subsequent ReverseGoodsIssue call. The chain becomes unrecoverable through standard paths. 
 6. Step 3 — Cancel WL-linked Blocked Stock (GRRV / MT107) 
 Fiori: Monitor Value Chains → navigate to the GRRV (MT107) document → Cancel 
 ⚠️ The Cancel button only appears AFTER Step 2 ( ReverseGoodsReceipt ) is complete. It is not present before that — do not look for it earlier. 
 This step removes the WL-linked GR blocked stock at the receiving plant. It must be performed before Step 5 (Delete IBD) and before Steps 5–7 can succeed. 
 API status: ❌ M7/492 — WL-linked document cancellation via API_MATERIAL_DOCUMENT_SRV is blocked. Monitor Value Chains is the only viable path. 
 7. Step 4 — Cancel Post GI from Issuing SiT (GIIV) 
 Fiori: Monitor Value Chains → navigate to the GIIV document → Cancel 
 Same pattern as Step 3. While in Monitor Value Chains on the STO header, find the GIIV row in the Documents panel, click its Navigation arrow button to open the detail view, then use the Cancel button in the header toolbar. 
 This step cancels the GIIV process step. It must be completed (together with Step 3) before Steps 5–7 — without it, OBD OverallGoodsMvtStatus remains C after Step 6, causing Step 7 DELETE to fail with VL/066. 
 API status: ❌ — no OData equivalent. Monitor Value Chains UI Cancel is the only path. 
 ⚠️ UI5 button behavior: Standard DOM element.click() silently fails on SAP UI5 controls. Use Playwright browser_click via snapshot ref (real mousedown/mouseup) or sap.ui.getCore().byId(id).firePress() as fallback. 
 8. Step 5 — Delete Inbound Delivery 
 Prerequisite: Steps 3+4 (GRRV and GIIV Monitor Value Chain Cancels) complete. IBD OverallGoodsMovementStatus = A . 
 API: ✅ DELETE via API_INBOUND_DELIVERY_SRV with If-Match: * (HTTP 204). 
 $ibd = "<IBD_NUMBER>"
$cookieJarIBD = "$env:TEMP\ibd_$(Get-Date -Format 'HHmmss').txt"

# Fetch CSRF token
$fetchOut = & curl.exe -s -D - -o NUL `
 -u "${user}:${pass}" `
 -H "x-csrf-token: fetch" `
 -H "Accept: application/json" `
 -c $cookieJarIBD `
 "$ibdRoot/A_InbDeliveryHeader"
$csrf = ($fetchOut | Select-String "(?i)x-csrf-token:\s*(.+)").Matches.Groups[1].Value.Trim()

# DELETE IBD
& curl.exe -s -X DELETE `
 -u "${user}:${pass}" `
 -H "x-csrf-token: $csrf" `
 -H "If-Match: *" `
 -H "Accept: application/json" `
 -b $cookieJarIBD -c $cookieJarIBD `
 -w "`nHTTP_STATUS:%{http_code}" `
 "$ibdRoot/A_InbDeliveryHeader('${ibd}')"
# Expected: HTTP 204 (no body) 
 Verify deletion: GET the IBD → expect HTTP 404 "Resource not found". 
 ⚠️ VL/066 on DELETE means Steps 3+4 were incomplete. Complete GRRV and GIIV Monitor Value Chain Cancels first, then retry. 
 9. Step 6 — Reverse Goods Issue on OBD 
 Service: API_OUTBOUND_DELIVERY_SRV (OData V2) 
 Prerequisites: 
 Step 2 (GR Reversal) complete: IBD OverallGoodsMovementStatus = A 
 Steps 3+4 (GRRV and GIIV cancel) complete 
 Step 5 (IBD deleted) complete 
 Step 1 (IV2 cancelled) complete: OBD OverallIntcoBillingStatus = A 
 Verification before calling: 
 # Confirm OBD billing status is A and all IV2 documents are cancelled
& curl.exe -s -u "${user}:${pass}" `
 -H "Accept: application/json" `
 "$obdRoot/A_OutbDeliveryHeader('<OBD_NUMBER>')?`$select=OverallIntcoBillingStatus,OverallGoodsMvtStatus&`$format=json"
# Required: OverallIntcoBillingStatus = 'A' 
 API call: 
 $obd = "<OBD_NUMBER>"

$cookieJarOBD = "$env:TEMP\obd_$(Get-Date -Format 'HHmmss').txt"
$fetchOut = & curl.exe -s -D - -o NUL `
 -u "${user}:${pass}" `
 -H "x-csrf-token: fetch" `
 -H "Accept: application/json" `
 -c $cookieJarOBD `
 "$obdRoot/A_OutbDeliveryHeader"
$csrf = ($fetchOut | Select-String "(?i)x-csrf-token:\s*(.+)").Matches.Groups[1].Value.Trim()

# ReverseGoodsIssue — do NOT include If-Match (returns HTTP 501 if added)
& curl.exe -s -X POST `
 -u "${user}:${pass}" `
 -H "x-csrf-token: $csrf" `
 -H "Accept: application/json" `
 -b $cookieJarOBD -c $cookieJarOBD `
 -w "`nHTTP_STATUS:%{http_code}" `
 "$obdRoot/ReverseGoodsIssue?DeliveryDocument='${obd}'&ActualGoodsMovementDate=datetime'<REVERSAL_DATE>T00:00:00'&`$format=json"
# Expected: HTTP 200 
 Fiori alternative (after IBD deleted): Reverse GI – Outbound Delivery (VL09) also becomes available once the IBD is deleted in Step 5. 
 🔑 OBD status after this call: When Steps 3+4 Monitor Value Chain Cancels were completed first, OBD.OverallGoodsMvtStatus correctly updates C→A after this call, unblocki

title: End-to-End Principal Propagation for AI Agents with SAP Integration Suite, MCP and SAP Cloud Connect
author: Nacho_Munoz
text:
Can AI agents access enterprise APIs using the actual end-user identity instead of a shared technical account? 
 In this PoC, I implemented end-to-end Principal Propagation using SAP Integration Suite MCP Server, SAP Cloud Connector, OAuth 2.0 and X.509 certificates, reaching a custom non-SAP backend. 
 The result: cryptographically verified user identity, backend-enforced authorization and real VERIFIED evidence. Four orders existed, but the AI agent could access none because the authenticated user lacked permission. 
 This article covers the architecture, configuration, technical challenges and security lessons learned along the way.

title: Business AI in ABAP Cloud - Embedding AI with the ABAP AI SDK (Part 2)
author: fabianfellhauer
text:
Business AI in ABAP Cloud - Embedding AI with the ABAP AI SDK (Part 2) 
 Cheers ABAP Folks! 
 In my last blog post , we discussed the high-level strategy for implementing business AI capabilities in ABAP Cloud. We looked at the two pillars, Embedded AI in ABAP and Agentic AI via Joule , and when to use which approach. If you haven't read it yet, I'd recommend starting there for the bigger picture. 
 Today, we're going hands-on. This post dives into Embedded AI, the capabilities that run directly inside your ABAP application, powered by the ABAP AI SDK . We'll walk through the fundamentals, introduce the SDK, and then look at two concrete use cases using everyone's favorite business scenario: Trip & Expense Management . 
 Yes, trip & expense management. We all love it, don't we? Nothing brings more joy to a business traveler than filling out expense reports after a long trip. So, let's see how AI can take some of that joy... I mean burden ... away. 

 The Fundamentals: Connecting ABAP to AI 
 Before you write a single line of AI-related ABAP code, you need to get the plumbing right. All embedded AI scenarios in ABAP Cloud require a connection to SAP AI Core , specifically to the Generative AI Hub that provides access to Large Language Models (LLMs) hosted by hyperscalers. 
 This connection is established via Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM) , a framework that allows you to manage and operate AI scenarios in a standardized, transportable way. Think of ISLM as the lifecycle backbone: it handles connectivity, model deployment, prompt management, and the runtime configuration that ties everything together. 
 Setting Up the Connection 
 The setup follows a straightforward pattern ( SAP Help, Set Up ABAP AI SDK powered by ISLM) 
 Subscribe to SAP AI Core in your SAP BTP subaccount and enable the required service plan. 
 Create a service instance and service key for SAP AI Core in the BTP cockpit. 
 Establish connectivity between SAP AI Core and your ABAP system by creating a communication arrangement based on communication scenario SAP_COM_0A69 . 
 This is a customer-managed outbound integration, which means you own the connection setup. Once established, ISLM can create and activate model deployments, and the ABAP AI SDK can execute prompts against the deployed models. For a detailed step-by-step walkthrough, I recommend the tutorial Set Up SAP BTP and Integrate SAP AI Core with ISLM on SAP Developers. 
 The ABAP AI SDK, Your AI Toolbox 
 With the connection established, let's talk about the tool you'll actually use in your ABAP code: the ABAP AI SDK . It's a typed, ABAP-native reuse library that provides access to generative AI functionality via ISLM. It is available across the full ABAP Cloud landscape, covering: 
 SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition & On-Premise 
 SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 
 SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment (Steampunk) 
 This means the same SDK, the same APIs, the same patterns, regardless of where your ABAP system runs. 
 What's in for me? 
 The ABAP AI SDK offers a set of APIs built around common LLM usage patterns: 
 Completion API – Send a prompt to an LLM and receive a generated text response. This is the core building block for most embedded AI scenarios. 
 Prompt Library API – Work with prompt templates predefined in ISLM, including parameterized prompts with runtime variable substitution. Very useful when you want to keep your prompts maintainable and out of your ABAP code. 
 Connectivity management – The SDK handles the connection to the Generative AI Hub transparently. You reference an intelligent scenario by name, and the SDK resolves the rest. 
 Exception handling – Typed ABAP exceptions, so you can integrate AI calls into your existing error handling patterns without reinventing the wheel. 
 The APIs are vendor-neutral, meaning the same ABAP code works regardless of which underlying LLM provider is configured in SAP AI Core. If your organization switches from one model to another, you change the configuration in ISLM, not your ABAP code. Your CTO changes their mind about the AI vendor? No problem, no code change required – ok, to be honest with you: The prompting might be polished most probably a little. 
 The Simplest Possible Call 
 To give you a feel for the developer experience, here's the simplest possible AI call using the Completion API ( SAP ABAP Cheat Sheets, Generative AI) " Get a Completion API instance for your intelligent scenario
DATA(ai_api) = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'Z_MY_SCENARIO' ).

" Execute a prompt and get the result
DATA(result) = ai_api->execute_for_string( `Classify this trip as customer-facing or internal.` ).

" Retrieve the generated text
DATA(completion) = result->get_completion( ). 
 Three lines of ABAP. That's it. The factory creates an instance tied to your intelligent scenario (which contains all the connection and model details), you execute a prompt, and you get back the LLM's response as a string. No HTTP client setup, no JSON parsing, no authentication handling. The SDK takes care of all of that. If you've ever tried calling a REST API from ABAP the "old-fashioned way", you'll know exactly how much boilerplate this saves you. 
 Of course, real-world scenarios are a bit more involved. You'll use prompt templates with parameters, handle exceptions, and integrate the result into your business logic. But the fundamental pattern stays the same. 
 Orchestration Capabilities 
 For enterprise-grade AI scenarios, the ABAP AI SDK also supports orchestration through the SAP AI Core Orchestration Service . This adds capabilities that are critical for production use: 
 Data Masking – Automatically redact sensitive information (personal data, financial details) before it reaches the LLM. Essential for data protection and GDPR compliance, and something your compliance team will thank you for. 
 Document Grounding – Enrich your prompts with business-relevant context from documents, reducing hallucinations and improving response accuracy. Because an LLM that confidently makes things up is entertaining at dinner parties, but not in your ERP system. 
 Content Filtering – Ensure that LLM responses are safe, appropriate, and compliant with your organisation's policies. 
 These capabilities are configured at the orchestration level, so you don't need to implement masking or filtering logic yourself in ABAP. It's handled for you. 

 Let’s get our hands dirty: Trip & Expense Management 
 For the rest of this blog post, we'll use a Trip & Expense Management application as our running example. Picture a RAP-based Fiori application where employees create travel requests, and after the trip, submit expense reports. 
 We'll tackle two concrete use cases: 
 Data Prediction with Fiori Input Assistance : Automatically categorizing a trip as "customer-facing" or "internal" based on the trip description. 
 Data Extraction from files : Extracting structured data (payment amounts, categories, etc.) from uploaded receipt documents. 
 Both are real-world scenarios that demonstrate different facets of the ABAP AI SDK. And both address the same fundamental truth: nobody enjoys filling out forms manually when a machine could do it better and faster. Let's start. 

 Use Case 1: Trip Categorization with RAP Recommendations 
 The Problem 
 When an employee creates a travel request, they need to fill out several fields: destination, purpose, cost center, and importantly, trip category (e.g. "customer-facing" or "internal"). This categorization drives downstream processes like approval workflows, budget allocation, and reporting. Today, users pick the category manually. They might get it wrong, or they pick whatever option is closest to the mouse cursor. What if the system could propose the right category automatically , based on the trip description? 
 The Solution: Fiori Input Assistance 
 This is exactly what Fiori Input Assistance implemented with RAP recommendations is designed for. RAP recommendations are a built-in input assistance feature in the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) that proposes field values for input fields on an SAP Fiori UI ( SAP Help, Defining RAP Recommendations ). Available since SAP BTP ABAP Environment 2602 and SAP S/4HANA Cloud 2602 , RAP Recommendations can be implemented using either deterministic rules or generative AI , and you can even mix both approaches in the same application. The key principles of RAP recommendations: 
 They are exposed in SAP Fiori as a recommendation pattern of type input assistance, meaning the user sees suggested values directly in the input field. 
 They are built on top of a value help, so you need an existing value help for the target field. 
 They are triggered by side effects: when the user changes a source field (e.g. trip description), the recommendation function runs and proposes values for the target field (e.g. trip category). 
 They integrate seamlessly with the RAP programming model. No custom UI development required. Zero. Nada. 
 Figure 1: Fiori Input Assistance implemented with RAP recommendations 
 How It Works: The Architecture 
 The implementation involves three layers: 
 Behavior Definition – Declare which fields receive recommendations and define the recommendation function. 
 Behavior Implementation – Implement the recommendation logic in the behavior pool, using the ABAP AI SDK to call an LLM for intelligent categorization. 
 Projection Behavior Definition – Expose the recommendations in the projection layer for the Fiori UI. 
 If you've built a RAP Business Object before, this will feel very familiar. It's the same layered pattern, just with AI sprinkled on top. 
 Step 1: Define Recommendations in the Behavior Definition 
 In your behavior definition, you mark the target field as relevant for recommendations, declare a recommendation function and define a side effect on which the recommendation function should be triggered. This tells the RAP framework: whenever the user changes the “ title ” field, execute function GetRecommendedValuesFunction and propose values for attribute “ type ”. The user types "Customer workshop in Berlin" and the system immediately suggests "Customer-facing". It almost feels like the system is reading the user's mind, except it's reading their input field. define behavior for ZR_AITRIP alias Trip
{
 //Define for which fields an recommendation output is generated

 //Define the recommendation function itself
 recommendation function GetRecommendedValuesFunction;

 //Define the trigger (e.g. other context field)

 executed on field Title;
 }
} 
 Step 2: Implement the Recommendation Logic 
 In the behavior pool, you implement the recommendation function. This is where the ABAP AI SDK comes in. You use the completion API to ask an LLM to categorize the trip based on the available context: 
 Read the current entity data (description, destination, etc.) 
 Build a prompt with the trip context, based on your system's master data 
 Call the ABAP AI SDK Completion API 
 Parse the LLM response 
 Return the recommended value(s) with scores 
 The recommendation function returns a list of proposed values, each with a score and a flag indicating whether it's the suggested (top-ranked) value. The Fiori UI renders these as input assistance. The user can accept, modify, or override the suggestion. The AI proposes, the human decides. As it should be.

title: Creating SQLScript Table Function views - the hard way
author: XaviPolo
text:
SAP Datasphere consultant has to create a SQL Scripting View (Table Function) with dozens of output fields, you can almost see their expression change. I have yet to meet someone who genuinely enjoys that task. 
 The reason is simple. SAP Datasphere is generally unable to derive the output structure of the generated function automatically (while this is certainly not a trivial capability to implement, it is also the kind of functionality one would reasonably expect from an enterprise-grade data platform), and as a result, the consultant is often forced to define the output structure manually by creating every field one by one, specifying data type, length, and other attributes individually. Repeat that process dozens of times, and what should be a simple development task quickly becomes a tedious exercise. 
 But Datasphere consultants are used to finding creative workarounds. 
 For a long time, there was a small trick that helped avoid this manual effort: 
 Create the object as a standard SQL View. 
 Paste the SQL statement that generates the desired output structure. 
 Validate the view so Datasphere generates the output schema automatically. 
 Change the view type to SQL Scripting (Table Function) . 
 Adjust the code by adding the RETURN statement and the final semicolon. 
 This approach could save several minutes of repetitive work and significantly improve the developer experience. 
 I say could because, for some time now, this workaround has stopped working reliably. In many cases it no longer works at all. 
 While reviewing SAP support incidents, I found SAP Note , which appears to be related to this behavior. Unfortunately, the note is quite generic. It mentions that output structure generation may fail for complex queries and even warns about the possibility of view corruption. It literally states: 
 "Avoid validating the SQL script prematurely during development to minimize the risk of corruption." 
 The recommendation leaves several open questions. What exactly constitutes validating "prematurely"? Why should pressing the Validate button at the wrong moment risk corrupting the view? And, more importantly, why is deriving the output structure still such a fragile process? 
 This brings us back to the original situation. Either consultants manually create the output structure field by field and lose valuable development time, or they wait until the new AI-assisted service becomes capable of handling SQL Scripting views reliably. Of course, the ideal scenario would be for the existing workaround to work consistently again, without requiring an additional paid service . 

 I'm curious to know how others deal with this when creating SQL Scripting (Table Function) Views. Do you define the output structure manually, or have you found a better workaround?

Through its “Group Finance Backbone” initiative, the company worked with SAP to harmonize finance operations across manufacturing, sales, and financial services. BMW Group established one integrated finance template supporting organization-wide reporting, standardized approximately 800 ground-level processes, and improved data comparability and granularity across 15 major source systems. 

 We believe customer outcomes like these demonstrate the importance of combining standardized processes, trusted data, and central governance to help global organizations improve transparency and prepare for future innovation.

 Finance leaders are balancing a growing range of priorities, from improving operational performance and managing risk to preparing their organizations for AI-powered innovation. title: The Gap That No LLM Can Close
author: Maarten Rikken
text:
Generative AI helps people to write, research, program, or evaluate content faster. A huge benefit, but one that also comes with a serious problem: according to a McKinsey study , while 80% of AI users report increased personal productivity, only six percent of companies say that AI significantly increased their operating profit. 
 Turn structured data into accurate, explainable predictions that your team and AI agents can act on 

 Learn more about tabular AI 

 How can this gap be closed? The answer lies in helping companies detect risks, defaults, losses, and liquidity pressures sooner—and manage them more effectively. 

 For Germany and Europe, it is not an abstract challenge, but the key to future prosperity. Our economic strength lies in industry: in mechanical engineering, in the automotive supply chain, in complex manufacturing and logistics processes. According to German Economic Institute estimates, AI can generate around €440 billion of additional gross value in Germany by 2034. 

 Good, but not in every case 

 To get the economy moving again, we need a different kind of AI. Because it is not enough to process and generate language; AI must also be able to deal with data that companies work with the most. And this is where common large language models (LLMs) reach their limits. Structured data—for example, numbers in tables—help companies understand what is happening right now and what may come next. 

 This requires AI models that understand the relationships among rows, columns, entities, and numbers. This is exactly what current research results show: several independent benchmarks from the year 2026 prove that even high-performance LLMs perform significantly weaker in table reasoning tasks—for example, in the ability to draw conclusions from tables and to recognize relationships—than in language tasks. 

 When data anticipates what’s next 

 Tables follow their own logic. Values do not stand next to each other in isolation, but in relationships between columns, rows, timeframes, and business transactions. Accordingly, tabular AI is designed to recognize patterns across columns as well as in the associated tables that make up a company system. The real added value lies in this networked context. Looking at a customer ID in isolation is one thing. Seeing which orders this customer places and predicting warehouse requirements from these data is a completely different thing. 

 A practical example: a manufacturer wants to identify early which customers are most likely to pay late. For this, a single piece of information is not enough. Among other things, relevant factors include payment history, order history, delivery data, and external industry information. Only the interaction of these data makes reliable predictions possible. That’s precisely what tabular AI models are built for. 

 What this means for AI investments 

 Classic machine learning methods are still used in many companies today for predictions based on structured data. They often deliver good results, but typically have to be developed, trained, and operated separately for each individual application: one model for demand forecasting, another for payment default risks or for prioritizing sales contacts, each with data preparation, training, monitoring, and ongoing maintenance. 

 Tabular foundation models change this equation. They do not have to be redeveloped for every business question but are universally applicable. This creates an immense scaling effect. In the future, instead of hundreds of specialized models, a single one—such as SAP-RPT-1.6, which we have just made available to customers—will suffice. With this, companies can build on historic examples and existing patterns from their business data in order to identify new risks and opportunities at an early stage. 

 For companies, this means a concrete shift: AI predictions will no longer have to be developed as complex individual projects in the future. In other words, the path from a specific question to the universal use of a model for any questions becomes shorter and cheaper. 

 In addition, since tabular foundation models are not pre-trained on individual use cases, but on large amounts of data, they can also recognize patterns across different use cases that specialized individual models, especially in limited data layers, often overlook. Therefore, in addition to the scaling effect, there is also a gain in knowledge, which previously did not exist in the analytical processing of tabular data. 

 New category for enterprise AI 

 At SAP, we are working on the next level of enterprise AI. With the acquisition of Prior Labs in July , we are further accelerating this path: combining Prior Labs’ basic research with the corporate reality of our customers, and the experience of SAP in the application of AI in business-critical business processes. 

 With TabPFN-3 , Prior Labs has developed one of the most powerful open-source models for tabular predictions. Together with the tabular foundation models of the SAP-RPT family and SAP Knowledge Graph, this creates an infrastructure that securely generates structured predictions directly from the company-specific data with the individual business context. 

 In general, now we are seeing a trend toward various types of foundation models. In addition to tabular foundation models, models that have been trained on the basis of time series—for example, a large number of measurements—are being created. You can evaluate the measurements, recognize patterns, and thus also predict numerical values over time. 

 Conclusion 

 The first wave of generative AI is making employees more productive. The next one can make companies more forward-looking. The decisive factor here is not whether companies use LLMs or tabular foundation models. It is crucial to combine the two where they provide the greatest benefit: LLMs for interaction with language and knowledge, tabular models for forecasts based on structured business data. 

 Done right, AI becomes more than a productivity tool. It becomes a driver of better business decisions—and a foundation for a stronger economy.

title: 1,000 AI Agents by SAP TechEd: SAP and Partners Accelerate Together
author: Andrea Diederichs
text:
When SAP issued a challenge to its partner ecosystem ahead of SAP Sapphire in 2026, it set an ambitious goal: 100 to 200 partner-built AI agents before the event opened its doors. What happened next surprised everyone. 
 SAP partners can help you bring out your best 

 Learn how 

 By the time SAP Sapphire kicked off in May, partners had delivered over 680 agents built on SAP Business AI Platform —more than triple the original target. 

 For SAP Chief Partner Officer Karl Fahrbach, the number was not just a data point. It was a signal. “That talks about the power of the ecosystem,” he said. 

 That momentum is now being channeled into the next challenge. SAP has since raised the bar, setting a new target of 1,000 partner-built agents ahead of SAP TechEd . This time, building an agent is not enough. The focus is to deploy partner AI agents at SAP customers, providing them real business value with measurable business outcomes. 

 Redefining what “good” looks like 

 Behind this fundamental change, SAP is challenging traditional notions of growth and redefining the path to partner success. For years, the dominant metric was transactional: how much did a partner sell, how many projects did they deliver. That model, Fahrbach said, is no longer sufficient: “We need to start measuring the partners on real customer outcomes, not how many projects they deliver, but what the customer has really achieved: cost savings, top-line growth, or process efficiency.” 

 This reflects a broader change in customer expectations. A year ago, the question customers were asking was: what can AI do? Today, it is: what business outcome can AI deliver? The experimentation phase is over. “That’s what we’re hearing from many customers, and it’s exactly where partners have an important role to play,” Fahrbach said. 

 The shift also extends to how customer outcomes are delivered. “Customers don’t want large implementations anymore,” he explained. “They are increasingly seeking AI to help them run faster and leaner with their projects so they can get to value much sooner. That’s the perfect foundation for becoming an Autonomous Enterprise .” 

 The €100 million fund: early traction 

 A €100 million investment fund SAP announced at SAP Sapphire for partners that build and successfully deploy AI agents is now drawing submissions. The fund is designed to both accelerate customers’ adoption of AI and attract a new generation of AI-native companies into the SAP ecosystem. Demand has been significant, with nearly 1,000 customers expressing interest. As of October 1, more than 500 customers had been confirmed, and more than 400 partners had signed up to participate. 

 “We’re seeing strong interest from new partners in the fund,” Fahrbach confirmed. “It adds another element of appeal for new partners to join the already strong and thriving ecosystem.” 

 The evidence for that pull was already visible on the SAP Sapphire show floor, where Fahrbach noted a shift: a new cohort of AI-native startups appeared alongside the established system integrators—companies that were, in his words, “born in the AI world.” 

 But the initiative is not only intended to bring new partners into the fold; it also reflects SAP’s commitment to the partners that have helped build the ecosystem over decades. Fahrbach said SAP is committed to helping all its partners enhance their AI capabilities and capitalize on emerging opportunities to thrive in an AI-driven market. 

 Where partner agents will live 

 While many SAP partners have already developed agents for SAP, it’s now about making those agents visible and deploying them with customers. To date, over 120 partner-developed agents are published on SAP Discovery Center , and by the end of this year, the number is forecasted to rise to more than 300 partner AI agents, showcasing the power of the SAP ecosystem. 

 One of the structural changes shaping the ecosystem concerns how customers find and provision partner-built agents. SAP has created a seamless discover-to-operate experience by bringing partner agents directly into the SAP AI Agent Hub, which plays a central role for agent discovery, governance, and lifecycle management alongside SAP’s native agents. SAP AI Agent Hub is free of charge for customers managing up to 500 AI agents, and already governs agents across hundreds of companies. 

 “SAP AI Agent Hub allows customers to view SAP and partner agents in a single marketplace,” Fahrbach said. “They can browse, select, and provision partner-developed agents as easily as they do SAP’s own. Partner agents are integrated into the experience on equal footing with ours.” 

 The push toward SAP TechEd 

 To reduce barriers ahead of SAP TechEd, SAP is offering a range of incentives to its partner ecosystem. Qualifying partners can receive complimentary conference passes, enabling developers and consultants to gain hands-on experience with SAP Business AI Platform. 

 SAP is also providing free access to the new Joule Studio solution for the SAP Early Adopter Care program customers through the end of 2026. More than two dozen partners are currently contributing to the SAP Early Adopter Care program. Joule Studio introduces a new paradigm of intent-based development , enabling users to create applications and solutions by describing what they want to achieve, rather than writing code manually. This significantly lowers the technical barrier to application development and accelerates innovation. 

 A key attraction at SAP TechEd will be the Agent Lab, where partners can gain hands-on experience building with SAP’s latest technologies, including Joule Studio. The goal is to move beyond product demonstrations and enable participants to build and experiment with real solutions. 

 “We want developers and consultants to come to SAP TechEd and gain real, hands-on experience with the platform,” Fahrbach said. “Not just to observe, but to build, experiment, and leave with something they can immediately put into practice.” 

 The push to accelerate partner enablement is supported by an already significant skills investment. The SAP ecosystem now includes more than 200,000 cloud-certified consultants and over 38,000 business AI-certified professionals, creating a deep bench of expertise as the company expands its AI ambitions. 

 To help partners navigate quality standards, SAP has introduced a partner validation program for SAP Business AI Platform with certification and development requirements, and a review process that agents must pass before they qualify for distribution. 

 Where the differentiation lies 

 Increasingly, the value of AI is being strengthened through industry differentiation by partner, with AI that understands not just a function like procurement or finance, but procurement in automotive, finance in pharmaceuticals, or supply chain in retail. Generic AI may drive productivity, but industry differentiation by partner drives competitive advantage. That is where partners, with their deep knowledge of specific sectors and micro-verticals, can create the most differentiation. 

 An AI strategy built on partners 

 With the fund now active, a 1,000-agent target on the board, and partner agents embedded directly in the SAP AI Agent Hub, the stage is set. SAP TechEd will be the first major test of how quickly the ecosystem can translate that vision into tangible outcomes. The message from SAP is unambiguous: the future of its AI strategy will be built in partnership. 

 “SAP cannot do it alone,” Fahrbach says. “Our partners are essential. They provide the speed, scale, and specialized expertise needed to bring AI innovation to SAP customers.” 

 SAP Chief Partner Officer Karl Fahrbach 

 Karl Fahrbach has led SAP’s partner ecosystem since 2019, when he became the company’s first chief partner officer. He has grown the SAP ecosystem to nearly 7,000 partners that build, sell, and deploy cloud and AI solutions from SAP. 

 Before shaping the ecosystem from the top, Fahrbach spent years building it from the ground up: he joined SAP in 2006 as part of the team that created the company’s flagship SAP PartnerEdge program, having previously worked at Microsoft and Oracle. Today, he is focused on mobilizing the SAP partner ecosystem as the force multiplier that will accelerate the Autonomous Enterprise and scale the AI agents at its core.
